deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is a pencil draft of §§16-18 of Riemann's Inaugural Dissertation (Göttingen 1851), 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse'. That is the section where Dirichlet's principle is stated and used. The page has one right-side-up line at the top. The rest is written with the sheet turned 180° and is heavily struck through, so only fragments can be read with confidence. What follows is a reconstruction of the argument those fragments belong to, set against the published text. Where I fill gaps, I say so.

(0) Top line (right way up): '...wie durch Abänderung in einzelnen Punkten hebbaren Unstetigkeit'. This continues the previous page (§16). Riemann distinguishes two kinds of discontinuity in the admissible functions λ:
- discontinuities along a line make the Dirichlet-type integral L infinite;
- discontinuities at isolated points can be removed ('gehoben') by changing values at single points, so they are harmless.
The radial computations on the previous page serve this point. There he works with ∫(λ-λ0)^2 + (∂λ/∂ρ)^2 ρ dρ dφ and integrates by parts: ∫(λ')^2 dρ = -∫λ λ'' dρ. Their purpose is to show that the integral can be forced above any bound C near a line discontinuity, but not near a point.

(1) Setting (my restatement from the published dissertation). T is a surface spread over the plane. α and β are given functions. λ ranges over functions that vanish on the boundary and are continuous except at isolated points. Define
Ω(λ) = ∫_T [ (∂α/∂x - ∂β/∂y + ∂λ/∂x)^2 + (∂α/∂y + ∂β/∂x + ∂λ/∂y)^2 ] dT.
Or, in the simpler form used in the draft, L(u) = ∫_T |∇u|^2 dT with u = α + λ, i.e. u has prescribed boundary values.

(2) Existence, read from the inverted text: 'Es ist aber hier zu zeigen, dass, wenn auch λ unendlich ... wird ...'. Riemann wants to show that admitting λ which become infinite at isolated points does not spoil the argument. Such λ still give finite L. Since Ω ≥ 0 and Ω is finite for some λ, he concludes there is a λ = u at which Ω attains a minimum. The '3. 11. 10.' at the foot of the inverted text is most plausibly a cross-reference to earlier articles. It might also be a date; this is unclear.

(3) First variation. The fragments '∂u/∂x, ∂u/∂y ... = 0 ... in einzelnen Punkten' and '∂φ/∂x = 0' fit the standard step (filled in by me):
Ω(u + hη) = Ω(u) + 2h ∫(u_x η_x + u_y η_y) dT + h^2 ∫(η_x^2 + η_y^2) dT.
Minimality forces the linear term to vanish for every admissible η with η = 0 on the boundary. Integrating by parts (Green) gives ∫ η Δu dT = 0, hence Δu = 0, i.e. ∂X/∂x + ∂Y/∂y = 0, wherever u is regular. Isolated points are handled by the removability remark in (0).

(4) Uniqueness. Readable fragments: 'u ≦ u′ ... u′ ≦ u, folglich u = u′' (probably about the Ω-values: Ω(u) ≤ Ω(u′) and Ω(u′) ≤ Ω(u)), 'u + λ ... u + λ′', and '... Rand = 0 und ... constant'. Reconstruction (mine): suppose u and u′ = u + w are both minimizers with the same boundary values. Then:
- by (3), the cross term ∫∇u·∇w vanishes;
- so Ω(u′) = Ω(u) + ∫|∇w|^2;
- equality of the two minima gives ∫|∇w|^2 = 0;
- hence w_x = w_y = 0, so w is constant;
- w = 0 on the boundary, so w ≡ 0.
This matches the last sentence of the next page: 'immer für eine und nur für eine dieser Functionen ein Minimum'.

Overall purpose: this is the existence and uniqueness of a harmonic function (or of the complex function u + iv) with prescribed boundary data or discontinuities, via Dirichlet's principle. It feeds the Riemann mapping material of §21ff, which the next page begins ('Geometrisch stellt sich eine stetige Function W ... als eine Abbildung ... dar').
errors: The existence step (Ω ≥ 0 and finite, therefore a minimizing function exists) is the well-known gap in Dirichlet's principle. The infimum need not be attained in the admissible class. Weierstrass criticized this (1870; cf. his counterexample); Hilbert repaired it (1900/1904). The draft shares the gap of the printed dissertation.

The draft is fragmentary and heavily corrected, so no individual computational slip can be verified on this page. The uniqueness argument as reconstructed is correct, given the existence of a minimizer and the vanishing of the first variation.

The claim that point singularities are removable needs care. Functions such as log log(1/r) are unbounded at a point yet have finite Dirichlet integral (allowed, consistent with 'wenn auch λ unendlich wird'). A point singularity of a harmonic function such as log r, however, gives an infinite Dirichlet integral. The argument tacitly relies on this distinction.

results.what: Discontinuities of λ along a line make the Dirichlet integral infinite; discontinuities at isolated points are removable and harmless
results.modern_name: Sobolev H^1 functions have no jump across curves (trace theory); points have zero capacity in 2D
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1851 dissertation (informal); made rigorous in 20th-century potential theory and Sobolev space theory

results.what: Existence of a minimizer of the Dirichlet integral among functions with prescribed boundary values
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Thomson (Kelvin), Dirichlet; named and used by Riemann 1851/1857; rigorous proof by Hilbert 1900

results.what: Vanishing of the first variation implies Δu = 0 (Euler–Lagrange equation of the Dirichlet integral)
results.modern_name: Weyl's lemma / Euler–Lagrange equation for Dirichlet energy
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Gauss, Green, Dirichlet); in this form Riemann 1851

results.what: Uniqueness of the minimizer: ∫|∇w|^2 = 0 and w = 0 on the boundary imply w ≡ 0
results.modern_name: Uniqueness for the Dirichlet problem via energy method

deep.surprise_reason: This is a working draft of §§16-18 of Riemann's published 1851 dissertation (Dirichlet principle, removable point singularities, uniqueness). The content is well known as his. Interest is limited to genesis details, such as his worry about λ becoming infinite at isolated points.

checkable.asserts: Equals 1/log(2), which is finite: a function unbounded at a point (log log 1/r) has finite Dirichlet integral in 2D, so point singularities of λ need not spoil finiteness.
Equals 1/eps, which tends to infinity as eps→0: smoothing a unit jump across a line over width eps gives Dirichlet energy ~ 1/eps per unit length, so line discontinuities give infinite L.
Equals infinity: the harmonic point singularity log r has infinite Dirichlet integral.
Equals 0: the pointwise identity behind Ω(u+hη)=Ω(u)+2h∫∇u·∇η+h^2∫|∇η|^2.
Equals 0: integration by parts ∫(λ')^2 = -∫λλ'' for λ vanishing at the endpoints (used on the preceding page).

transcription_corrections: The line read as '... u = u′, folglich u = u′' appears to be an inequality pair, roughly 'u ≦ u′ ... u′ ≦ u, folglich u = u′'. It most likely refers to the Ω-values of two minimizers.

The phrase '... Rand = 0 und ... constant' near the inverted 'top' (the physical upper part of the page) belongs to the uniqueness conclusion: the difference function is constant and vanishes on the boundary.
'3. 11. 10.' at the foot of the inverted text is likely a cross-reference to earlier articles (or possibly a date), not a formula.

Near the 'Ω' fragment the expression involving ∂Y/∂x, ∂X/∂y (and ∂u/∂x, ∂u/∂y) belongs to the first-variation computation. The right-side-up top line should read 'wie durch Abänderung in einzelnen Punkten hebbaren Unstetigkeit'.
